BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: The area will continue to sit under broad west-southwest flow Monday through midweek.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Above normal temperatures through the weekend.
- A weak cold front brings a slight chance of showers to Baker County and the west central Idaho mountains on Sunday.
- Significantly above normal temperatures develop next week, peaking Wednesday around 15 degrees above normal with potential record highs.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A generally quiet weather pattern will prevail across southeast Oregon and southwest Idaho through the weekend as a weak upper level ridge remains over the Great Basin. Patchy valley fog and low stratus remain possible Saturday morning in sheltered low- lying basins.

Mostly clear skies on Saturday will allow for strong surface heating, with afternoon highs climbing into the mid 60s throughout the Treasure Valley. Developing south to southeasterly winds will also aid in local warm air advection and boundary layer mixing, boosting temperatures to at least 15 degrees above normal for early November.

High and mid level clouds will increase Saturday night into Sunday as a weak shortwave trough and associated cold front track across the Pacific Northwest to our north. Moisture will remain largely limited to the northern tier, supporting around a 10 percent chance of light precipitation over Baker County and the West Central Mountains on Sunday. Despite increased cloud cover and the weak frontal passage, temperatures will remain unseasonably mild, topping out at least 10 to 12 degrees above normal across the region.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: The area will continue to sit under broad west-southwest flow Monday through midweek. On Monday, a weak Pacific shortwave trough will pass over north-central ID, bringing small chances of precipitation over the northernmost mountains of our CWA late Monday into early Tuesday. Otherwise, a highly amplified Pacific ridge will build into the western CONUS Tuesday through Thursday, continuing dry conditions and temperatures 10 to 15 degrees above normal. Come Friday, there is general guidance agreement of an incoming upper low from the Gulf of Alaska digging into the Pacific northwest region, keeping our area under a strong southwest flow. There is considerable uncertainty over the arrival of precipitation over our area. For now, Friday will see slight chances of rain and mountain snow and the beginning of a slight cooldown.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Ensemble guidance is in excellent agreement (unfortunately) of above normal temperatures and overall dry conditions lasting through the end of next week due to the upper level ridging in place.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Very light snow showers possible (10-20% chance) this afternoon in the high country, with any snow amounts less than 1".
- Above normal temperatures and dry conditions are expected Saturday through late next week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: We will be entering a prolonged relatively quiet period after today and likely through the end of next week as upper level ridging will reside over the western United States. For us, that will mean overall dry conditions and above normal temperatures.

Today, light snow showers are possible (10-20% chance) mainly for the I-70 mountain corridor and surrounding areas above 8,500-9,000 ft this afternoon and evening. However, with overall lack of decent moisture, snow accumulations will be a dusting to <1" at best. Across the plains, one last day of seasonal temperatures are expected today, with forecasted highs in the mid-to-high 50s (and likely low 60s for the far eastern plains).

This weekend and into beginning of next week, upper level ridging will continue entering the region with a cut-off low spinning over southern Arizona/New Mexico. With weak northerly flow aloft over Colorado, we won't have access to the moisture from that system and instead will receive drier air. This will keep precipitation chances near-zero for our whole forecast area. In terms of temperatures, it sure won't really feel like fall, with temperatures expected to reach 10-13 degrees above normal. 700-mb temps will reach up to 7-8 degrees C by Sunday and Monday, which roughly translates to surface temperatures in the high 60s to potentially low 70s by Monday.

Ensemble guidance is in excellent agreement (unfortunately) of above normal temperatures and overall dry conditions lasting through the end of next week due to the upper level ridging in place. We could see slightly "cooler" conditions (temperatures in the low 60s) on Wednesday as northerly flow aloft advects colder air into the region. However, we should warm right back up on Thursday. Towards next weekend, the upper level ridge could begin to break down, but model solutions vary on exactly when that will happen.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: The long term forecast for the Intermountain West is rather boring to say the least. Upper level ridging will put our region in a subsequent chokehold for the next 7 days. This is great news for anyone that needs to build a house or pour concrete this week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Near to just above average temperatures and mostly dry conditions are expected through the weekend.
-Breezier conditions return on Sunday into Monday, however fire weather conditions are not anticipated at this time.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Forecast remains on track as we remain in a warm and dry pattern heading into the weekend. Current GOES mid-level water vapor imagery shows a shortwave trough digging south and east across the Desert Southwest, bringing SE Wyoming and the Nebraska Panhandle mainly just a few mid and high level clouds. High temperatures today are forecast to remain slightly above average for this time of year, with locations along and east of the I-25 corridor expected to reach the mid to upper 50s this afternoon, with cooler temperatures in the upper 40s to low 50s west of the Laramie Range. For some perspective, the average high in Cheyenne for this day is in the low 50s. Expecting winds to remain rather calm today as we are under the influence of a 1027 mb surface anticyclone located over the Central Great Plains. Can expect another seasonably chilly night heading into the weekend as large-scale subsidence and weak isentropic descent is in place over the region, with skies remaining mostly clear. Wouldn't be surprised to see some areas of frost early tomorrow morning across the Panhandle, as high-resolution guidance indicates some lingering low-level moisture especially along the North Platte River Valley.

The weekend will start off on a similar note as a positively-tilted ridge begins to amplify over the western half of the country, with 500 mb height anomalies exceeding the 90th percentile relative to climatology. Given the building ridge, temperatures will again remain well above average, peaking in the low 60s east of the Laramie Range, and remaining mainly in the 50s to the west. An abundance of high clouds will be the limiting factor for stronger surface heating.

Heading into Sunday, the ridge axis will be located over our area, and will likely be our warmest day of the period. Wouldn't be surprised to see a few locations in the Nebraska Panhandle exceed the 70 degree mark, as NBM median temperatures are showing widespread upper 60s. Not expecting any records to be broken at this time, but it will feel unseasonably warm for early November. Sunday will also be noticeably windier compared to the previous couple of days, as zonal 700 mb flow increases to 35-40 knots. As it stands, in-house wind guidance keeps even our wind-prone areas well below high wind criteria, but conditions will still be gusty. No fire weather highlights are needed at this time as minimum RH values look to be 20-25% on Sunday afternoon, though any downward trends in low-level moisture will need to be monitored in future forecasts.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: The long term forecast for the Intermountain West is rather boring to say the least. Upper level ridging will put our region in a subsequent chokehold for the next 7 days. This is great news for anyone that needs to build a house or pour concrete this week. Sunday, looks to be the warmest day of the week in the long term forecast when the ridge looks like an amplified sine wave that advects in warmer but drier air into the region. High temperatures look to be in the mid 60's for areas east of I-25 with the potential of some areas to reach 70. 700mb temperatures look to peak around 6 or 7C which will also give us slightly warmer temperatures in the upper 30s overnight compared to the upper 20s we had the past several days. During the next work week, there will be multiple low pressure system moving up and over our ridge dragging some colder air with it. While these systems don't seem to currently present our region with precipitation chances. It will knock our high temperatures down to the more seasonable mid 50's to low 60's and overnight lows into the upper 20's to low 30's as 700mb temperatures hover between 0 and 1C.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: As high pressure materializes over the region, dry and milder weather will be on tap for the foreseeable future. This will give us a much needed break from the recent abundant precipitation.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A quick system will move through this afternoon, bringing an isolated shower to the higher terrain.
- Warmer and drier conditions highlight the rest of the seven- day forecast.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A shortwave trough is expected to move through the area today. This will bring some high clouds to the sky, with a chance for isolated showers over the higher terrain. Accumulations, if any, will be on the lighter side. Overnight cloud cover will moderate overnight lows and preclude the notion of any valley fog development. Beyond Friday night, the shortwave moves off to our east, with an expansive ridge of high pressure moving in from the west.

As high pressure materializes over the region, dry and milder weather will be on tap for the foreseeable future. This will give us a much needed break from the recent abundant precipitation. Looking ahead towards next week, some systems will be rotating near the PacNW, but as those traverse eastward, storm tracks remain north, keeping us in a drier period even longer. Daytime highs under this ridge will be seasonable, if not above normal at times.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Little change overall through the extended period for the forecast area, as broad high pressure ridge keeps the state dry and warm.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - High pressure aloft will keep dry and warm conditions in place through the extended forecast period.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Currently...Upper low dropping south into western AZ this afternoon was producing widespread mid and high level cloudiness across Colorado. Otherwise a very pleasant day across the region, with temps as of 11 AM in the 40s for the high valleys, and 50s across the plains. Temperature readings are forecast to warm another 2 to 4 degrees for most locations through the afternoon.

Tonight...Upper low to the southwest is expected to potentially produce a few isolated showers along the Continental Divide late this afternoon into early evening, with the best chance for anything across the southwest mts. Regardless, isolated POPs and bare minimum QPF means little if anything is likely to reach the ground. Plan on gradual lessening of the cloud shield through the overnight hours, with minimum temps in the 20s for the high valleys and 30s for the plains.

Saturday and Saturday night...Broad area of high pressure builds into the region, ushering in a period of dry conditions, lighter winds and warm temperatures residing right at or slightly above seasonal normals. Look for high temps tomorrow in the 50s for the high valleys, and upper 50s to mid 60s for the plains. Moore

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Little change overall through the extended period for the forecast area, as broad high pressure ridge keeps the state dry and warm. Extended models do agree on an upper shortwave crossing the ridge Tue evening, brushing by the forecast area and perhaps knocking a few degrees off high temps for Wed. Once that passes, the ridge becomes amplified over the Great Basin and Rocky Mt regions, keeping CO dry but open to passing waves brushing by to the east.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Models indicate potential for a chunk of northern stream energy to graze by northern Utah/ southern ID on Tuesday, introducing a cooler airmass that will help to bring potential for valley inversions to break or, at the very least, weaken.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Breezy winds will remain in place across far southwestern Utah around the Pine Valley Mountains, with peak winds expected to gust between 30-40 mph through Saturday morning.
- A stretch of dry and increasingly mild weather is anticipated over the weekend, with the dry conditions expected to continue for much of the upcoming week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A trough and its associated area of low pressure will continue to depart the forecast area through the next 12 hours, bringing increasingly stable conditions across Utah and southwest Wyoming. With high pressure building in from the north and low pressure departing to the south, an increased surface pressure gradient across southern Utah will help to drive stronger winds through terrain features (particularly in southwestern Utah). These breezy winds, specifically around the Pine Valley Mountains, will continue through the remainder of the evening and overnight hours, gradually tapering off through Saturday morning as the aforementioned area of low pressure continues its track south.

High pressure will spread across the area throughout the day on Saturday, bringing dry and stable conditions areawide. With warming temperatures overhead, anticipate a gradual warming trend through the weekend alongside largely clear skies. As we're getting further into the cool season, warming temperatures overhead begin to raise concern for persistent valley inversions. As such, would anticipate at least a little bit of valley haze along the Wasatch Front by the end of the weekend or the beginning of next week as this area of high pressure looks to remain in place through at least Monday.

Models indicate potential for a chunk of northern stream energy to graze by northern Utah/ southern ID on Tuesday, introducing a cooler airmass that will help to bring potential for valley inversions to break or, at the very least, weaken. This is going to be the most noteworthy impact of this weak shortwave as moisture is severely lacking. If the trough helps to break the inversion, then whatever urban haze has accumulated will have a chance to dissipate. However, if this wave comes in weaker and/ or tracks farther north, then we'll likely continue to see the accumulation of valley pollutants from now through the end of next week as high pressure looks to quickly reestablish over the region from mid-week forward.
Models do indicate strong potential for the pattern to shift/ break down as we head into late next week/ next weekend.

2660.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Chris Dickson
bottom_line: Generally safe avalanche conditions exist. Lower elevation slopes hold too little snow to produce avalanches, while snow on higher elevation slopes settles and weakens under continued mild weather.
Steer clear of stiff wind-drifted pockets of snow in the alpine, and beware of early-season hazards at lower elevations, such as shallowly buried rocks.

2747.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Andrew McWilliams
bottom_line: Most slopes hold too little snow to produce an avalanche. At high elevations, steer around areas of firm, drifted snow if you find them below ridges or in gullies.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.

(Precipitation data are recorded from Secesh SNOTEL site at 6540')

• December - 68" (12.6" SWE)

• February - 41" (5.4" SWE)

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Kreston Rohrig
bottom_line: Most slopes are generally safe for travel. If you find more than about two feet of snow on the ground or see evidence of recent wind-drifting on a steep slope, consider avoiding that terrain. Stiffer pockets of wind-drifted snow are common, like just below ridgelines and along gully walls. Because wind speeds have been light, the drifted snow may be softer and less obvious than the typical Colorado wind slab. Most slopes near and below treeline hold too little snow to produce an avalanche.
